There are two ways to enter an address, just a segment or a segment with an offset. For example, 2000 and 2000:0 or 2000:0000 are all the same location. At the top part of the screen the segment you are in will be shown. At the bottom part will be the current offset to the segment and the 8-bit value storedat the offset. This means when the microprocessor generates the write signal, the write enable will be activated and the value on the data bus will be written on the address location on address lines A1 through A10 within the RAM chip...
On the RAM chip, the RD signal is also connected to the OE, and since you can write to RAM, the WR signal is attached to the RAM's WE or Write Enable pin.
If the output enable is turned off, the output of the EPROM is effectively disconnected from the data bus. This is known as a
tri-state operation where the output is high impedance.

On the EPROM chip, since it is read only, the RD signal is connected to the OE or output enable pin of the EPROM chip. This means when the microprocessor wants to read data from the EPROM, the output enable is turned on...
When both lines are high, the microprocessor is neither reading nor writing to memory. Both lines cannot be low at the same time because the microprocessor can not read and write simultaneously...
If the WR line is low, the microprocessor is trying to write information to memory. When the RD line is low, the microprocessor is trying to read information from memory.
The last two control signals from the microprocessor to memory are the WR and RD. These are the read and write signals.
Normally, the IO/M signal is used to select between I/O space and memory. For the purpose of conserving space on the circuit board, the IO/M signal is not used with the system's memory.

A device known as a decoder is used to read address lines A12 and A13 and generate a low signal on an output line to turn a chip on. Below is shown the truth table for a decoder.
This method of using the additional address lines is known as chip select decoding. The available address lines to use are A12 through A15. In this 8085 system, only A12 and A13 are needed.

These address lines can address any location within each chip. The microprocessor can address 65 thousand locations. For this reason, the additional address lines are used to pick between the different chips..
A 11 is connected to the EPROM chip because it has more locations and needs extra address lines to access them. Remember that the EPROM is 4 Kbytes and the RAM is only
We need to look at the signals which are used to control the memory chips. A0 through A10 are connected directly to the A0 through A10 connections of all the memory chips.
The RAM contains 2 Kbytes of random access memory, known as the 6116 chip. As with the EPROM, 2 Kbytes times 8 bits equal 16 Kbits. This is where the 16 in the IC name comes from.
Since a byte is 8 bits, this chip holds 32 Kbits of data. This is where the 32 comes from in the IC name. Next to the EPROM is the location for 1 RAM chip.
The EPROM contains the monitor program which you use when the system is first turned on. It is made up of one chip, IC1, which is the 2732 chip. This chip contains 4 Kbytes of read only memory...

There are two types of memory attached to the 8085 microprocessor. The first type is EPROM memory, or Erasable Programmable Read Only Memory. This memory is programmed by a special device and cannot be changed without other special devices...

Now that you know how the address information is made available and how data information is amplified, let's look at how the memory chips are attached and controlled by the microprocessor...s
The buffer is active when the enable pin is low. This is important when another device has taken control of the bus. The signal will ensure that all other signals are disconnected from the data bus.
The buffer is enabled if either the RD or WR signal is low. This is achieved using two NAND gates to form an AND gate. The output of an AND gate is low if any input is low.

If the microprocessor was reading data from memory, information would flow from the right side to the left. For this condition, the S1 signal will be high indicates a READ operation is being performed...

If the microprocessor is writing data to the data bus, the S1 signal will be low. S1 low indicates that the microprocessor is trying to write. This tells the buffer to amplify signals from the left side and make them available on the right side...

The data buffers are controlled by the S1, RD and WR of the microprocessor. The chip containing the buffers is IC2, the 74HC245 chip. The S1 signal determines the direction of data flow through the buffer...
Remember, they need to be bi-directional because data slows from either the computer to memory or memory to the computer.

The address and data signals provided by the microprocessor are not strong enough to make it very far away from the actual microprocessor. While address output signals from the latch are strong enough, bi-directional buffers are needed for the data information..

It is important to note that the latches are not bi-directional. Address information is only generated by the microprocessor. If other devices need to indicate addresses to the microprocessor, they will pass it through the data lines just like any other data.

The ALE signal is put low which doesn't allow the latch outputs to change as the data is put on the lines. The data is then sent on the address/data pins. This makes all information available at one time...

When the address is on the lines, the address latch enable (ALE) signal goes high instructing the latch to take the inputs and make them available at the outputs. Now the microprocessor is ready to put the data information on the multiplexed lines..
The address latch, as its name implies, is used to latch an address.
However, the address information at the beginning of an instruction cycle needs to be available at the end of the cycle.

To accomplish this, the address is made available at the beginning of the operation and the data at the end of the cycle. Since data is the last information, it doesn't need to be saved in temporary memory...
For instructions that use memory, the microprocessor must have a method of multiplexing address and data information.

The address and data lines which come out of the microprocessor must be both demultiplexed depending on the signal and amplified. Address/Data lines, AD0 through AD7, are the lines that carry both data and addresses. The two information forms must have the capability on being separated (demultiplexed)....

In other microprocessor systems, another chip is required to generate the clock. The 8085's design eliminates this necessity, thereby reducing external circuitry.

The capacitors are used to filter out other frequencies, known as harmonics, from the crystal. Harmonics are frequencies which are multiplies of some base or fundamental frequency. These are not needed in the system and could cause noise...
